reading.body:
Precision agriculture has commercial AI deployments, federal adoption data, and a UN benchmarking framework operating at the same time.

The pattern is a layered ecosystem rather than a single vendor. Deere, CNH Industrial's Raven division, and pure plays like Carbon Robotics and Monarch ship vision-guided spraying, driverless tractors, and laser weeding as farm equipment. Bayer's Climate FieldView and Corteva's Granular turn soil, weather, and yield data into planting prescriptions. Planet Labs, Descartes Labs, and EarthDaily supply the satellite imagery those models consume, while AgGateway and AEM set the data and machinery standards that make the feeds interoperable.

What makes this notable for AI is that adoption is measured, not guessed. USDA ERS publishes precision-agriculture adoption series, Census BTOS covers agriculture-adjacent sectors in its AI-use series, FAO benchmarks digital agriculture globally, and AgFunder indexes venture funding. That measurement layer means deployment can be checked against real yield and income impact rather than model demos. The data does not cover compute, power, or building constraints, and it gives no adoption percentages, revenue figures, or energy use.

summary: Precision agriculture - vision-guided spraying, yield prediction, autonomous equipment - is deployed at commercial scale. Who tracks it: federal adoption data, a UN benchmarking framework, a venture index, and standards bodies, layered over the equipment giants and AI pure-plays actually shipping it.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey puts AI use in agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting at 6.2% of firms in the latest period, with the prior period suppressed. That is the only measured adoption figure in this material, and it covers firms answering yes to whether they used AI in the last two weeks. The sector's own measurement layer sits elsewhere: the USDA Economic Research Service publishes data series on precision-agriculture adoption across US farms, including variable-rate technology, yield monitoring and autonomous equipment, and the FAO's digital agriculture program, with the 60 Decibels-supported Digital Agriculture Index, benchmarks platform adoption and real-world yield and income impact globally.

What AI is deployed for in this sector, according to the sources here, clusters around a few concrete jobs. Carbon Robotics describes its LaserWeeder and Carbon Autonomy as physical AI for agriculture, with a Large Plant Model trained on what it calls the world's largest agricultural dataset collected by LaserWeeders, aimed at reducing costs, eliminating weeds and increasing yields. John Deere's precision agriculture line, including See and Spray and autonomous tractors, is described here as the reference commercial deployment. Bayer's Climate FieldView turns soil, weather and yield data into planting and input prescriptions, and the page reports that farmers using FieldView seed scripts saw an average increase of +5 bu/ac compared to users who wrote their own scripts. CNH Industrial's Raven division builds driverless tractor technology, AI path-planning and precision application. Planet Labs supplies daily satellite imagery and derived data products that feed yield prediction and crop-stress detection.

Money and vendor concentration show up in two places. AgFunder reports that global agrifoodtech funding hit $16.2 billion in 2025, almost flat versus the prior year at -3%, with investors writing checks more selectively toward companies with tangible science, real unit economics and clear paths to revenue. It also reports that funding in developing markets grew 63% between 2023 and 2024 against a 4% decline in global agrifoodtech, that APAC startups raised $4.2 billion as of the end of October 2024, a 38% increase on the $3.1 billion raised over the same period in 2023, and that African agrifoodtech raised $145 million in the first half of 2024, a 1.6% year-over-year increase representing just 1.6% of global investment, after a 2023 in which African investment declined 62% to $275 million. On the vendor side, the large platforms named here are Bayer's Climate FieldView and Corteva's Granular, with Deere, CNH and Raven at the equipment layer and pure-plays like Carbon Robotics and Monarch attacking single problems.

The supporting institutions are mostly standards, science and data bodies rather than AI vendors. AgGateway is a non-profit promoting the industry's transition to digital agriculture, and its Traceability Initiative in North America works on seeding and provenance including grain traceability, while in Europe it is standing up a special interest group on farm and crop field identification to link crop data across industry sources through standard identifiers, with stated benefits in product management, customer service, food safety and regulatory compliance. The Association of Equipment Manufacturers covers autonomous machinery, AI hardware standards and robotics adoption across crop and livestock production, and organizes events and advocacy for equipment manufacturers. The International Society of Precision Agriculture connects academic research on remote sensing and spatial analytics to commercial practice. The World Economic Forum's 100 Million Farmers initiative aims to move one in five of the world's farmers to regenerative and climate-smart practices by 2030, mainly through financing and collaboration models, and does not track AI itself, though its goals of soil health, water, resilience and farmer income are the outcomes most farm AI tools claim to improve.

On risk and regulation, the material is thin. AgGateway's traceability and identification work is framed partly around food safety and regulatory compliance, and AEM describes bringing agriculture OEMs together to shape policy and combat environmental, political and economic changes facing agriculture. Beyond that, the sources here do not describe a regulatory posture specific to AI in farming, and no source reports a compliance requirement, liability finding or enforcement action.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material supports a few practical readings. Measured AI use among agriculture firms is low at 6.2% per the Census Bureau, so adoption is early rather than universal. The deployments that are described are narrow and task-specific, weed elimination, spraying, path planning, seed scripts and prescriptions, rather than general-purpose systems. The one quantified outcome in these sources is Climate FieldView's reported +5 bu/ac average increase for farmers using its seed scripts versus writing their own. Capital is available but selective per AgFunder, and the data plumbing, standards and interoperability through bodies like AgGateway, plus the satellite and sensor layers, is what the models depend on. Where the sources are silent, on ROI beyond that single figure, on regulation, and on farm-level costs, this material does not fill the gap.

https://climate.com/.brief: Climate FieldView describes itself as an all-in-one digital farming solution for making data-driven decisions, with a separate version built for dealers that combines field data with their expertise. The page states that farmers using FieldView seed scripts saw an average increase of +5 bu/ac compared with users who wrote their own scripts. It also describes FieldView Drive 2.0, which it says can send seed scripts without a thumb drive, has built-in GPS, syncs data faster and works with a wider range of equipment. Other parts of the page point to farmer case studies, support for field trials, and planning checklists.

https://www.aem.org/.brief: AEM describes itself as an association that advances construction and agriculture equipment manufacturers in the global marketplace, and says it works across four areas: advocacy, safety, trade shows and events, and market data. It says it owns and organizes events that connect members with customers worldwide, and that its advocacy work covers grassroots campaigns, public affairs and research. AEM states it is holding a Momentum event in 2026 in Gainesville, GA, intended to deepen connections and deliver industry insights. It also says thousands of industry peers subscribe to its Industry Advisor publication for updates about equipment manufacturing.

https://www.ispag.org/.brief: The International Society of Precision Agriculture is a scientific organization that develops technologies to help feed the world and improve quality of life. It offers a definition of precision agriculture in more than fifteen languages and gives members access to directories, networking, and discounted conference registration. Members receive a monthly “ISPA newsletter” that shares news, job listings, and event information, and the society is preparing for the 17th ICPA and 11th ConBAP in summer 2026. Country Representatives promote ISPA worldwide; applicants must email info@ispag.org with a bio, CV, and be current members, and members can post job announcements on the site and in newsletters.

https://www.planet.com/.brief: Planet Labs offers a platform called Planet Insights that brings together daily satellite imagery, derived data products, and cloud-based tools in one place. The company claims its imagery is the highest-frequency commercial Earth observation data, enabling daily monitoring, high-resolution tasking, and deeper derived insights. It says the platform lets users view the planet in time, space, and frequency, helping them make decisions quickly and confidently. Planet reports that organizations across many sectors use the platform to address operational challenges with a global, dynamic perspective.

https://www.ers.usda.gov/.brief: The Economic Research Service publishes State Fact Sheets covering population, income, poverty, food security, education, employment, farm characteristics, farm financial indicators, top commodities and agricultural exports, according to the agency, with data for all states, metro and nonmetro breakouts within states, and Puerto Rico where applicable, plus county-level links where available. It also offers a Food Price Outlook with food price data and forecasts of changes in the Consumer Price Index and Producer Price Index for food. A separate Vegetables and Pulses Data collection provides statistics on fresh and processed vegetables and dry pulses in the United States, along with some global data for those sectors. The service says readers can subscribe to an e-mail notification service for announcements of its latest reports and other news.

https://agfunder.com/research/.brief: AgFunder reports that global agrifoodtech funding reached $16.2 billion in 2025, down 3% year-over-year, with investors becoming more selective and favoring companies demonstrating "tangible science, real unit economics, and clear paths to revenue." While overall funding remained relatively flat, regional patterns diverged significantly: developing markets agrifoodtech grew 63% between 2023 and 2024, Asia-Pacific startups raised $4.2 billion as of October 2024 (a 38% increase), and African agrifoodtech showed mild recovery with $145 million raised in the first half of 2024 after a 62% decline in 2023. These trends suggest a sector undergoing consolidation, with capital concentrating in regions and companies meeting stricter investment criteria.

https://www.fao.org/digital-agriculture/.brief: The Global AgriInno Challenge 2026 finished its first stage, with 13 youth-led solutions chosen from 137 valid entries among 191 total applications, earning a place at a final pitch event in China. The page describes e-Agriculture as a global community of practice supporting dialogue and information exchange on using information and communication technologies for sustainable agriculture and rural development. It states that e-Agriculture grew out of Action Line C7 on ICT applications from the World Summit on the Information Society, with the Food and Agriculture Organization assigned as facilitator of that action line and of the community of practice. The page also notes FAO took part in Geneva in the 8th CEOs & Global Leaders Forum of the International Coffee Organization, contributing to a session on collective data initiatives, and reports farmers in Maiwand district, Kandahar province, using greenhouse cultivation and drip irrigation, including Tela Mohammad, who manages a 400-square-metre greenhouse shared with five other farmers.
